query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a low concentration (~0.3–0.5 atomic percent) of interstitial carbon to a tungsten‐based refractory HEA will trigger the in‐situ formation of a uniform dispersion of coherent nano-carbide precipitates. These carbides will, in turn, both provide precipitation strengthening and refine the microstructure so as to activate additional plasticity mechanisms (e.g., TRIP/TWIP), thereby simultaneously increasing yield strength while delaying localized failure and enhancing ductility relative to the undoped alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-based refractory HEA processed via stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) that exhibits a high-strength bcc matrix with coherent nano-precipitates, as typically reported (e.g., with ~2.15 GPa tensile strength and 15% ductility).
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, low-level carbon doping (approximately 0.3–0.5 at.%) during alloy synthesis and subsequent thermo-mechanical processing.
generation.conditions: Standard ambient temperature tensile testing after SCCPs processing; carbon concentration must be maintained below the threshold that would produce excessive, brittle carbides, and the processing conditions should promote a fine, coherent dispersion.
generation.structural_mediator: A fine, uniformly distributed network of coherent nano-carbide precipitates within the bcc matrix that serves as both dislocation obstacles and nucleation sites for strain-induced transformations (e.g., twinning or martensitic phase formation).
generation.mechanism: Interstitial carbon encourages the nucleation of nano-carbides that are coherent with the matrix. These precipitates hinder dislocation motion (enhancing strength via the Orowan mechanism) while also refining the microstructure and triggering additional deformation mechanisms (such as TRIP/TWIP) that help delay crack initiation and propagation, thereby improving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to an undoped tungsten-based refractory HEA processed under SCCPs, the carbon-doped alloy should exhibit a moderate improvement in yield strength (e.g., approximately 10–20% higher) while maintaining or slightly increasing tensile ductility (improving uniform elongation by roughly 5–10%).
generation.baseline: The reference material is the tungsten-based refractory HEA with SCCPs that already shows ultrahigh strength (~2.15 GPa) with ~15% ductility.
generation.boundary: If the carbon level exceeds ~0.5 at.%, brittle carbide phases might form at grain boundaries instead of as coherent, well-dispersed nanoparticles, which would reduce ductility. Also, if processing conditions do not sustain fine, coherent precipitates, the twin-assisted or transformation-related plasticity mechanisms may not be activated, limiting the benefit.
generation.uncertainty: The exact carbon concentration window and processing parameters need further optimization. The hypothesis builds on evidence from studies showing that (1) interstitial atoms (carbon) can trigger cooperative TWIP/TRIP effects and nanoprecipitate strengthening in HEAs (e.g., PMC5227964) and (2) carbide formation in refractory HEAs can improve strength (e.g., PMC7517255). Extending these results to a tungsten-based SCCPs alloy involves uncertainty regarding the optimal carbon level and its interaction with the preexisting nanoprecipitate structure.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of tungsten-based refractory HEA samples with identical SCCPs thermo-mechanical processing parameters. One set will incorporate a controlled carbon doping of ~0.4 at.% while the control set will remain carbon-free. Perform uniaxial tensile tests at ambient temperature and conduct detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM/SEM) to verify the presence, distribution, and coherency of the nano-carbide precipitates.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., less than a 10% increase in yield strength and/or no preservation/enhancement of ductility) compared to the undoped control—or if microstructural analysis reveals the formation of coarse or brittle carbides rather than a fine coherent dispersion—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) consisting of multiple principle elements provide an avenue for realizing exceptional mechanical, physical and chemical properties. We report a novel strategy for designing a new class of HEAs incorporating the additional interstitial element carbon. This results in joint activation of twinning- and transformation-induced plasticity (TWIP and TRIP) by tuning the matrix phase’s instability in a metastable TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA. Besides TWIP and TRIP, such alloys benefit from massive substitutional and interstitial solid solution strengthening as well as from the composite effect associated with its dual-phase structure. Nanosize particle formation and grain size reduction are also utilized. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEA thus unifies all metallic strengthening mechanisms in one material, leading to twice the tensile strength compared to a single-phase HEA with similar composition, yet, at identical ductility.

In this work, the effect of dilute C-doped with a concertation of 0.1 at.% in RHEA master alloy was studied under both ambient pressure and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. Under low pressure, the XRD of RHEA with/without C shows the formation of pure BCC phase and lattice constant of 3.210 Å, indicating that the low concertation of C has an ignorable effect on the alloy phase and the crystal structure of RHEA. However, the doping of C has noticeable a impact on the hardness values of the RHEA. At a high pressure of 6 GPa, Ta3C and Nb3C Carbide with FCC_L12 phase appear when the temperature is above 809 °C. The carbides of Ta3C and Nb3C are very stable even when temperature increased to above 1000 °C. As carbides are usually shown and favorable in high-temperature structural materials in the form of hard constitutes in metal matrix composites, the mechanical properties of carbon doped master alloy RHEA might be improved after a combined high-pressure and high-temperature process.
